name: Philippe Pétain
role: Chief of the French State at Vichy (1940–1944)
summary: Philippe Pétain concentrated executive and legislative power in his own office after France’s defeat in 1940. His National Revolution promoted traditional family roles and state-supervised cooperation between employers and workers. He pursued collaboration with Nazi Germany and personally tightened the first Vichy statute excluding Jews from public life.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Pétain retained armed forces for the French State and placed them under his command in Constitutional Act No. 2.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Constitutional Act No. 7 empowered Pétain to enforce administrative internment and detention in fortresses.

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: Pétain’s Labour Charter made wage payment for work the basis of employment, specifying a wage floor and supplements linked to occupation and output.

abortion-legal.rationale: Pétain’s February 1942 law subjected habitual or commercial abortion providers to administrative internment and proceedings before the State Tribunal.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: Article 4 of Pétain’s draft constitution protected private ownership arising from work and family saving, subject to public-purpose expropriation with compensation.

armed-resistance-to-occupation.rationale: Pétain adopted and maintained collaboration under German occupation and condemned resistance operations against the occupier as terrorism.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Constitutional Act No. 2 let Pétain issue budgetary and tax provisions on his own decision during a serious crisis.

class-collaboration.rationale: Articles 2 and 5 of Pétain's Labour Charter required collaboration between occupational groups and prohibited both strikes and employer lockouts.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Articles 31 and 56 of Pétain’s Labour Charter put wage negotiations and pay scales above the state minimum into the hands of organized occupational representatives.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Pétain exercised constituent powers himself and issued constitutional acts under his own authority after the July 1940 delegation.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Pétain's Labour Charter assigned industry committees a role in collective agreements and in setting the pay scales above a government-set minimum.

democracy-best.rationale: After taking office Pétain indefinitely adjourned the elected chambers and vested legislative authority in his own office, which was not subject to a popular vote.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Pétain assumed the headship by constitutional act in July 1940 and subsequently provided for succession without a direct popular election.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Pétain’s October 1940 law generally excluded married women from new public-sector employment and made exceptions for circumstances including inadequate spousal income.

duties-before-rights.rationale: The 1944 draft bound citizens to obedience, contribution to public expenses and civic obligations that could extend to sacrificing their lives for France.

elective-rulers.rationale: Pétain originally named an individual successor and later provided for an appointed interim college, with constituent authority returning to the National Assembly on his death in the absence of a ratified constitution.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Constitutional Act No. 7 let Pétain impose sanctions including administrative internment on senior officials for breaches of fidelity and official duties.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Pétain personally tightened a statute that defined Jews by ancestry and excluded them from public posts and several occupations on that basis.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Pétain’s Labour Charter established wages differentiated by professional qualification, individual output and working conditions above a subsistence floor.

ethnicity-statistics.rationale: Pétain's 2 June 1941 registration law required people classified as Jewish under the accompanying ancestry-based statute to declare that status to the authorities.

harm-principle.rationale: Pétain’s Labour Charter required participation in the expenses of state-organized occupational bodies and prohibited strikes and lockouts, even without an individualized showing of harm.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Pétain's Constitutional Act No. 2 placed command of the armed forces in the office he held.

head-of-state-dissolves-parliament.rationale: Pétain’s draft vested a power of dissolution in the president to use when he judged the relationship between government and nation required it.

independent-unions.rationale: Pétain's Labour Charter mandated a single union for each occupational category in a given area and put the statutes of national federations under ministerial approval.

individual-rights-only.rationale: Article 5 of Pétain’s draft constitution explicitly recognized the rights of spiritual, family, occupational and territorial communities.

leader-cult.rationale: Under Pétain’s rule education officials ordered his portrait displayed in classrooms, presenting him to pupils as the father and saviour of France.

legal-duty-to-work.rationale: Article 8 of Pétain’s September 1942 law required medically fit men in the covered age range to demonstrate that they held a job serving the country’s needs, and Article 2 provided for compulsory work assignments.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Pétain’s Price Charter put price limits on production and distribution, and the Labour Charter reserved economic allocation to newly established industrial bodies.

money-backed-by-precious-metals.rationale: Pétain proposed reserving gold for settling foreign accounts and determining the domestic money supply by the needs of production.

more-religion-public.rationale: Vichy gave religion a larger place in public life under Pétain through religious elements in schooling and by allowing public funding for houses of worship in December 1942.

national-rebirth.rationale: Pétain dismantled parliamentary government and undertook a programme of institutional and moral reconstruction explicitly called the National Revolution.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: The January 1941 law introduced optional religious instruction on public school premises, and the March 1941 law moved optional instruction off school premises.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Pétain adjourned both chambers indefinitely and exercised legislative power as head of state.

party-controls-media.rationale: Under Pétain’s government Vichy set up state information and censorship offices, and officials issued press instructions suppressing parts of the testimony at the trial Pétain initiated at Riom.

patriotic-education.rationale: Under Pétain the school authorities paired his official portrait and radio addresses with classroom materials and songs glorifying him as the saviour of France.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Pétain’s October 1940 programme called for France to preserve and continue to spread the Greek and Latin cultural inheritance he identified as its own.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Pétain’s October 1940 Price Charter authorized limits at all stages of distribution of agricultural goods and food during wartime shortages.

price-controls-fight-inflation.rationale: Pétain’s October 1940 Price Charter froze prices and empowered prefects to cap them at the wholesale and retail levels.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Under Act No. 7 Pétain gave himself power to impose disciplinary sanctions including internment without a judgment from the ordinary courts.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Under Pétain the February 1941 family allowance law increased payment rates for families with three or more children.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Article 4 of Pétain’s draft justified private property by the social function it gave its holder.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Articles 54 and 55 of Pétain's Labour Charter set a subsistence wage floor for employees doing normal work, adjusted to the local cost of living.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Pétain's Labour Charter bound industrial and commercial enterprises to occupational regulations and corporative decisions governing wages, hiring and dismissal.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Article 5 of Pétain's Labour Charter expressly prohibited strikes.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: At Pau Pétain attributed France’s thrift, patience and spiritual balance to its farming population and made rural life a model for the country’s renewal.

second-chamber.rationale: Pétain’s draft constitution provided for a Chamber of Deputies and a Senate, with part of the Senate chosen through occupational representation.

separate-church-state.rationale: The December 1942 amendment to the church–state separation law expressly allowed public authorities to finance buildings used for public worship.

separated-powers.rationale: Constitutional Act No. 2 gave Pétain full governmental power and enabled him to exercise legislative power while the chambers were suspended.

small-step-social-reform.rationale: Pétain displaced the operating institutions of the Third Republic and suspended both parliamentary chambers within days of receiving constituent authority.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Pétain used the July 1940 constitutional acts to displace parliamentary government with a new French State headed by his own office.

state-harmful.rationale: Pétain constituted a French State with governing, legislative and military powers vested in his office.

state-supports-good-ways-of-life.rationale: Pétain’s government used family benefits and restrictions on public employment to promote a household in which married women concentrated on home and family.

strong-leader.rationale: Pétain used his July 1940 constitutional acts to adjourn the chambers and make their reconvening depend on his permission while assuming legislative and executive power himself.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Pétain suspended political parties and ordered former leaders including Léon Blum and Édouard Daladier detained for life before their ordinary trial opened.

traditional-family.rationale: In his May 1941 address Pétain described the household and mothers' upbringing of children as necessary to France's survival and moral strength.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Pétain presented French national unity as stretching continuously across ten centuries in his October 1940 address.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Pétain's government made the Chantiers de jeunesse compulsory for twenty-year-old men in the unoccupied zone, with eight months of collective physical and civic training.

unions-run-economy.rationale: Pétain’s Labour Charter reserved economic decisions for industrial organization committees and subordinated the occupational organizations to directions from public authorities.

voluntary-union-payments-at-work.rationale: Articles 44 and 45 of Pétain's Labour Charter required contributions from all members of the profession and directed employers to withhold them from wages.

vote-at-sixteen.rationale: Pétain’s draft set a voting age of twenty-one for national and local elections.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Pétain told farmers at Pau that he wanted to increase the number of family farms and enable wage earners to become farm operators.

women-suffrage.rationale: Article 21 of Pétain’s draft gave qualified women the vote but confined eligibility for the national chambers to men.

worker-ownership.rationale: Article 2 of Pétain's Labour Charter retained employers as a distinct category and vested managerial authority in them by virtue of their social, technical and financial responsibilities.

notes: The audit focuses on Pétain’s exercise of power in 1940–1944. It treats the January 1944 constitution as an unpromulgated proposal and checks its provisions against the constitutional acts that actually governed Vichy. The first and second Jewish statutes and the separate identification law were checked against archival copies or official gazettes. Ancestry-based exclusion from employment and official registration settle different questions from residential segregation, citizenship at birth, and general immigration ceilings. The wartime reduction in civil protections and the Riom proceedings establish a record of repression. Germany’s own orders, and positions voiced only by Laval or Darlan, were not attributed to Pétain. The August 1942 age-of-consent measure distinguished same-sex relations from opposite-sex relations without criminalizing same-sex relations generally between people both of the then age of majority. Searches covered government and civil liberties (parliament, succession, courts, political repression, press), society and culture (religion, education, family, divorce, exclusion and citizenship), economy (occupational organization, living costs, farm ownership, price and monetary policy), world and globalism (armistice, resistance, colonial ties and foreign cooperation), means (regime change and opposition), ecology (resource and land policy) and technology (industrial policy and technical development). Searches in the French legal corpus were limited by its predominantly postwar coverage. World and globalism, ecology, and technology remain sparsely documented against these particular statements.
